paras: The lynching of three alleged horse thieves near Kirbyville, Missouri, took place in mid-April 1882, when vigilants hunted down three men accused of leading local horse stealing and hanged them at a pinery outside town. The men were not named, and no paper gave their race. Wire reports called it the first triple hanging in that part of Missouri in several years, and later dispatches placed it within a weeks-long vigilante pursuit of a horse-thief gang.

According to a special dispatch from Kirbyville, residents of the neighborhood had for some time been troubled by the depredations of horse thieves. St. Louis mail advices likewise said that a good deal of horse stealing had been done lately in that section, one of the southern counties of the state.

Three men were identified as the ringleaders, hunted down, taken to the pinery some distance from town, and hanged. The Ottawa Free Trader dated the hanging to April 14, while the St. Louis advices said only that it had happened a few days before April 15. The vigilants were said to have acted swiftly and dispersed the moment the men were swung up, leaving much excitement behind. The men's names were unknown, but they were said to have come from Greene county, Missouri.

A Little Rock special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on May 22 reported that a band of vigilants had been chasing eight horse thieves for over two weeks, of whom three had been lynched near Kirbyville. Of the other five, one had since been killed, one mortally wounded and one jailed, and the last two were said to be hemmed in on White river, where the dispatch predicted they would be captured and lynched. A Kentucky paper later reported that the gang had been broken up by local farmers, with all but two lynched or imprisoned.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the vigilants appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press on April 15 by two routes: a Chicago special that came by way of Little Rock, and mail advices from St. Louis. The Alexandria Gazette carried only a brief notice of a "triple lynching," adding that there was some doubt about the truth of the story and that it was under investigation. Other papers ran the fuller account as fact, under heads such as "Lynched" in the Rock Island Argus and "Horse Thieves Come to Grief" in the Memphis Public Ledger.

Weekly digests in New Jersey and elsewhere reduced it to a single line, that three horse thieves were captured near Kirbyville and hanged to trees. The Ottawa Free Trader placed it under "Thriving Business of Judge Lynch," beside the lynching of two Black men in Alabama, and, like the other papers, called the dead "thieves" without qualification. The May Little Rock report circulated widely in late May and early June, sometimes headed "Hunting Horse Thieves."

Accounts differ on timing: the Chicago special said the hanging had just occurred, the St. Louis advices said a few days earlier, and one paper gave April 14. The later reports also differ on the length of the vigilante chase, given as over two weeks in one version and three weeks in another.
